device: DuoCo-protocol LED strip, as measured 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-03 on Joe's two units

colour_byte_to_light.what: relative light emitted for a commanded byte, white (r=g=b), firmware brightness pinned to 100%. Normalised so byte 255 = 1.0.
colour_byte_to_light.measured_from: 15ms/iso3200 only, the one exposure of the three that spans the encoding (luma 1.8 to 209 of 255)

exposures_disagree.what: 5ms/iso800 relative to 15ms/iso3200 once both are put on the known exposure x ISO scale. 1.00 would be agreement.
exposures_disagree.why: the 5ms take never rises above luma 61, so the whole curve sits in the bottom quarter of the encoding where undoing sRGB does not undo what the ISP did. pwm_duty.csv reads 32% low at luma 17.5 and 60% low at luma 5.7 against a near-linear stimulus, which is the same shortfall.

colour_byte_to_light.caveat: the bottom few bytes are a lower bound on the light, not a measurement of it: byte 6 and below read under luma 20, where the pwm_duty check shows a 30-60% understatement. The shape above byte 8 is sound; a specific low-byte value is not.
colour_byte_to_light.supersedes: response_stitched.csv, which put half the output at byte 40 with no dark floor subtracted and so counted the wall the strip was lighting

firmware_brightness_to_light.what: the strip's own brightness setting, measured two independent ways
firmware_brightness_to_light.notes: 1% and 2% emit identically - the setting has no effect below 3%. These four points double as the check that catches the imaging pipeline crushing shadows; see colour_byte_to_light.exposures_disagree.

channels.what: whether driving one colour channel disturbs the others
channels.verdict: independent - the measured share of each channel holds constant as the driven channel is swept, so there is no level-dependent mixing to model

transition.what: does the firmware jump to a new colour or glide to it

write_path.what: how many of the app's writes reach the strip, and how fast
write_path.ceiling_model: delivered = min(offered, 1000 / (pacing_ms + 9)), the 9ms being write turnaround. Below that ceiling nothing is lost at any pacing.
write_path.ceiling_cause: the app's own per-device write pacing (DeviceWriteManager, default 50ms), not BLE and not the strip
write_path.strip_own_limit_note: with pacing out of the way the app offered 107-111Hz and the strip acked 76-79 of it, while everything at or below 89Hz survived intact. The hardware is roughly six times faster than the 50ms default has ever let it be.
write_path.over_driving_penalty: offering far more than the ceiling costs throughput and adds multi-second stalls: 502Hz offered for 15 minutes delivered 67.5Hz in lumps, with 441 stalls over a second and 664s of the 904s run stalled. Asking for 89Hz delivered a clean 89Hz.
write_path.second_device_costs: nothing - each device gets its own full ceiling

latency.what: command handed to the BLE stack -> light changes, both on one clock
latency.note: midpoint of the frame bracket. A crossing-frame figure - which is what was quoted before this analysis - is biased high by half a frame interval.
latency.source: latency_summary.csv (the run whose exposure was locked)

cct.what: whether the strip's native warm/cold channels can be driven directly
cct.verdict: yes, at sub-mode 0x03 only. Sub-modes 0x01 and 0x02 emit nothing at any warm/cold combination.
cct.supersedes: the earlier reading of cct_sweep as 'no light at all', which was the wrong sub-mode byte rather than a missing white channel
cct.app_impact: none. DuoCoProtocol.createCctCommand sends 0x02, but it is called only from CalibrationSequences - the app's warmth slider goes through RgbIntent.SetWarmth, which converts to Kelvin to RGB and sends an ordinary colour command. Nothing shipping is broken.
